title_en: The Night the Satellites Went Dark
description_ru: Выдуманная новость о магнитной буре, отключившей спутниковую навигацию, и пожилом смотрителе маяка, который вручную вывел суда в порт.
text:
PORT CALLOWAY, Northern Marches. For nineteen hours last Tuesday, the satellite navigation network that guides everything from container ships to pizza scooters fell silent across the entire coast of the Northern Marches, and the small harbour town of Port Calloway discovered that its most valuable navigational instrument was a seventy-three-year-old retired man named Edmund Thwaite, together with a lamp that the district council had spent a decade attempting to decommission.

The outage, which the national space weather bureau has attributed to a geomagnetic storm of unusual ferocity, left more than two hundred vessels without positioning data along a stretch of coast that sailors have nicknamed the Widow's Comb. Fishing smacks, a freighter laden with citrus fruit and a flotilla of amateur yachtsmen taking part in the annual Gannet Regatta found themselves groping through a blanket of sea fog with instruments that insisted, in serene and authoritative voices, that they were currently in the middle of a Saharan dune.

"It was extraordinary," said Harbour Master Ingrid Valtonen, who has served in the post for sixteen years and has seldom been surprised by anything except the budget. "One moment we had a modern coastal approach. The next, a hundred skippers were on the radio sounding like lost schoolchildren on a coach trip, and several of them were asking, with a certain dignity, whether we could possibly tell them where Wales had gone."

Salvation arrived, improbably, from the Skerrow Head lighthouse, which was automated in 1994 and has since been maintained chiefly by cormorants. Mr Thwaite, its last resident keeper, had been invited there only a week earlier to attend a sentimental ceremony marking its impending conversion into a luxury hotel, with a spa, a cocktail bar and, according to the brochure, "an authentic maritime atmosphere, without the inconvenience of authentic maritime work." When the first distress calls came through, he did not wait for instructions. He drove to the headland in his neighbour's van, climbed the one hundred and forty-two steps, bypassed the dormant electronics with a spanner and a bottle of olive oil, and cranked the great Fresnel lens into rotation by hand.

"I hadn't done it for thirty years," he told reporters afterwards, rubbing a shoulder with the air of a man who has been assured that he will not recover. "My knees complained all the way up. But the lamp, I am pleased to say, remembered exactly what to do."

For the next sixteen hours, assisted by two teenage volunteers and a flask of lukewarm tea, Mr Thwaite kept the beam sweeping across the dark. The old foghorns, silent for a generation, were coaxed back into service by a team of retired engineers whom the lighthouse association had hastily summoned, and who spent the night shouting technical instructions at one another over the din, in the manner of men who have waited many years to be indispensable. One by one, the vessels crept homeward, guided by the oldest navigation technology in the world: a bright thing on a rock, announcing, quite unambiguously, "Not here."

No casualties were reported. The regatta's eventual winner, a schoolteacher named Priya Okonkwo-Hale, admitted that she had reached port by "following the sound of a man shouting about washers." The freighter's master, who confessed sheepishly that he had spent four hours steering toward what proved to be a salmon farm, was escorted to his berth without damage to either party, though several fish are understood to be suffering from shock. A spokesman for the farm declined to comment, but a statement from its management expressed, in tones of dignified restraint, "deep concern about the reliability of modern seafaring."

The episode has reopened an awkward debate in the district. The council, which is expected to vote next month on the sale of the lighthouse to a hospitality group, now faces a petition bearing more than six thousand signatures, demanding that the building remain in public hands and, preferably, in working order. Councillor Rufus Abernethy, who had previously described the lamp as "a rusting liability with a sentimental following," has issued a statement saying that his remarks were "taken in a spirit different from that in which they were intended," which constituents have interpreted as an apology of a kind.

The hospitality group has been unexpectedly gracious. Its chief executive, Dominic Farrow-Leigh, said that the company "would be honoured to preserve the lighthouse's functioning role within its vision," and added that the hotel might offer a "storm package" including a night of authentic emergency. When asked whether guests would be expected to crank the lens themselves, he said the proposal was "an exciting direction, subject to insurance."

Experts caution that the incident exposes a deeper vulnerability. Professor Leonie Hartmann-Osei, of the Institute for Coastal Resilience, noted that modern shipping has quietly abandoned redundancy, trusting a single technology that, as she put it, "is delivered from space by people who are very clever and not at all in charge of the Sun." She observed that several nations are now reviving the use of radio beacons and even sextants, and that a minor industry has sprung up in the sale of paper charts, which, she added, "do not require a software update and will never ask you to accept new terms."

For his part, Mr Thwaite is unmoved by the attention. He has declined an offer to appear on a breakfast television programme, an invitation to a civic banquet and a sponsored hat. He did, however, accept a new pair of knee supports from the grateful fishermen's cooperative, and a lifetime supply of tea from the Gannet Regatta, whose organisers are rumoured to be considering a trophy in his name.

Asked by a young reporter whether he believed that old technology could ever truly replace the modern kind, Mr Thwaite considered the question for some time, gazing out at the horizon with an expression of mild pity. "I don't think it's a question of replacing, my dear," he said. "It's a question of remembering where we keep the light switch." Then he went home to bed, where, according to his neighbour, he slept for twenty-two hours and was awoken only by the sound of the council, ringing to ask whether he might consider a part-time position.

questions.question: Who guided the ships to safety?
questions.answer: Edmund Thwaite, the retired lighthouse keeper.

questions.question: What did the freighter steer toward by mistake?
What does the petition demand?
questions.answer: That the lighthouse stay in public hands and in working order.
